evidence_basis.originality_note: All prompts, data values, instrument specifications and figure briefs are newly authored. The mapped P2 leaves ground controlled definitions, comparison of repeated sets, interpretation of precision and accuracy, instrument resolution and selection. Complete source-question contexts were reviewed so uncertainty propagation and later-topic calculations remain excluded.

question_set_contract.difficulty_progression: direct Lesson 6 retrieval, recognition of precise but inaccurate data, recognition of instrument resolution, separation of resolution from accuracy, numerical comparison of repeated sets, instrument selection using range and resolution, then a mixed zero-error and measurement-quality application

questions.prompt: From the previous lesson, distinguish a systematic error from a random error by the pattern each produces in repeated measurements, and state one suitable response to each error type.
A reference mass is 40.00 g. Four repeated readings are 40.36 g, 40.35 g, 40.36 g and 40.35 g. Which description is best?

options.A: The readings are precise and accurate
options.B: The readings are precise but not accurate
options.C: The readings are accurate but not precise
options.D: The readings are neither precise nor accurate

questions.prompt: A digital force meter changes its display in steps of 0.01 N. What is its instrument resolution?
Which statement about an instrument with very fine resolution is correct?

options.A: It must give an accurate value because it shows small steps
options.B: It must give precise repeats because it shows many digits
options.C: It can distinguish small changes, but precision and accuracy must be judged separately
options.D: It removes every systematic and random error from the measurement

questions.prompt: A reference strip has a true length of 8.00 cm. Two students each make four measurements. Student P records 8.12 cm, 8.13 cm, 8.12 cm and 8.13 cm. Student Q records 7.94 cm, 8.06 cm, 8.02 cm and 7.98 cm.

figure.purpose: Present both repeated data sets and the true value spatially without classifying either set
figure.brief: Create an original Cambridge-inspired black-and-white rectangular number-line diagram from 7.90 cm to 8.15 cm. Mark the true value 8.00 cm and plot the four P readings on one row and the four Q readings on another row. Label only P, Q and true value. Do not draw range brackets, means or quality labels.
figure.alt_text: Two rows of repeated strip-length readings are plotted around a true value of 8.00 centimetres.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the range of each student's readings.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean length obtained by each student.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Using the calculated ranges and means, compare the precision and accuracy of the two sets.

questions.prompt: A laboratory has a metre rule with maximum range 1000 mm and resolution 1 mm, calipers with maximum range 150 mm and resolution 0.1 mm, and a micrometer with maximum range 25 mm and resolution 0.01 mm.

figure.purpose: Make instrument range and smallest distinguishable step easy to compare without selecting an instrument
figure.brief: Create an original Cambridge-inspired black-and-white rectangular comparison card with simple line drawings of a metre rule, calipers and a micrometer. Beneath each, reproduce only the supplied maximum range and resolution. Do not add ticks, arrows, rankings, suitability marks or sample objects.
figure.alt_text: A comparison card lists the maximum range and resolution of a metre rule, calipers and a micrometer.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the smallest change in length that the calipers can distinguish.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A rod is about 124 mm long and its length must be read in steps of 0.1 mm. Select the most suitable instrument and justify the choice using both range and resolution.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A thin wire has diameter about 0.60 mm and changes of 0.01 mm must be distinguished. Select the most suitable instrument and justify the choice using both range and resolution.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why the micrometer's fine resolution does not by itself show that a diameter result is accurate.

questions.prompt: A reference mass has true value 24.39 g. A digital balance gives repeated indicated readings of 24.86 g, 24.88 g, 24.87 g, 24.86 g and 24.88 g. When empty, the balance reads +0.48 g. Its display changes in steps of 0.01 g.

figure.purpose: Combine a true value, repeated readings, a zero check and a display step in one neutral laboratory record
figure.brief: Create an original Cambridge-inspired black-and-white rectangular laboratory record card. Show true mass 24.39 g, five separate indicated balance readings, an empty-balance display +0.48 g and a note that the display step is 0.01 g. Do not calculate a mean or range, apply a correction, or label precision, accuracy, resolution or error type.
figure.alt_text: A laboratory record gives a true mass, five repeated balance readings, a positive empty reading and the display step.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean and the range of the five indicated readings.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the resolution of the balance. Then use the mean, range and true value to assess the precision and accuracy of the uncorrected readings.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use the empty-balance reading to identify the prior-lesson error, determine the corrected mean mass and explain the effect of the correction on accuracy and precision.
